planting.note: Cut all stems back nearly to the ground in late winter since this is a hard-pruned, late-flowering type that blooms entirely on the current season's growth.

directions: Bred in Estonia by Uno Kivistik and named for the Estonian word for romantic, this vigorous Jackmanii-type climber opens flowers so dark a purple they read almost black before settling into a rich deep violet, with pale yellow-green stamens providing contrast. It climbs quickly to cover a fence, arbor, or obelisk and flowers continuously from midsummer into early fall. Give it good air circulation since, like many viticella-derived hybrids, it can be prone to mildew in stagnant conditions, though it otherwise resists clematis wilt well and tolerates dry spells once established.

planting.note: Set container-grown plants with the crown buried a couple of inches to protect against wilt and winter cold, then give light pruning since it flowers on both old and new wood.

directions: Raised by Raymond Evison and named for the RHS show garden in Devon, this large-flowered selection carries velvety claret-red blooms with a bold crown of bright yellow anthers that stand out sharply against the deep petal color. It flowers over an unusually long window from late spring through summer and into early fall, making it reliable value for a single container or trellis. Its moderate ultimate size and award-winning reliability have made it a staple recommendation for gardeners wanting a large-flowered clematis without a sprawling vine.

common_name: Angelique Clematis (Pale Lilac-Blue Compact Patio Clematis)

planting.note: Keep the compact root ball shaded and evenly moist in its container or bed, since this short, shrubby grower has a smaller root system than vigorous climbing types.

directions: Part of Raymond Evison's compact Boulevard breeding line, this cultivar bears star-shaped, pale lilac-blue flowers with gently waved sepal margins and a light reddish-brown center around the anthers. It grows into a thick, shrubby mound rather than a sprawling vine, making it well suited to pots on a patio or small bed edge. Flowering begins in late spring and continues sporadically into late summer, giving a long season of color from a plant that needs very little space.

common_name: Dark Eyes Clematis (Velvety Near-Black Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Cut stems back hard to a few inches above the ground each late winter, since flowers form only on the current year's growth and old wood contributes nothing.

directions: Raised in Germany by Willem Straver, this viticella-type cultivar opens flowers so deeply saturated with violet-red pigment that they appear almost black, later softening to a rich velvety purple as the silvery stamens become more prominent with age. Its compact habit and modest ultimate height make it a forgiving choice for beginners growing in a large pot topped with a small obelisk. It blooms freely from midsummer into early fall and, being an easy-pruning group-three type, tolerates aggressive late-winter cutback without any loss of vigor.

planting.note: Grow in a large container or small bed with the roots kept cool and shaded, since this is a genuinely dwarf Boulevard-type selection rather than a climbing vine.

directions: Launched by Raymond Evison at the 2016 Chelsea Flower Show in tribute to garden volunteers, this cultivar produces lavender-pink, star-shaped flowers accented by a deeper purple-red central bar and a pom-pom of pale yellow stamens. It stays genuinely compact, making it one of the easier Boulevard types to fit into a small container garden or balcony planting. Expect essentially continuous flowering from early summer through the start of fall, with little need for staking given its modest size.

common_name: Tekla Clematis (Rich Rose-Red Ruffled Patio Clematis)

planting.note: Train young growth onto a trellis or obelisk in a large container, then prune hard each spring since blooms are carried only on new season's stems.

directions: This late large-flowered cultivar produces ruffled, rich rose-red to violet-red blooms with a darker central bar and creamy-white stamens, on a vine compact enough to suit a large pot near an entryway. Flowering begins in midsummer and continues steadily through fall, giving it one of the longer display windows among the large-flowered patio types. Because it belongs to the hard-pruned late-flowering group, cutting it back close to the base each spring keeps growth tidy without sacrificing bloom.

common_name: Amethyst Beauty Clematis (Velvety Plum-Purple Compact Clematis)

planting.note: Cut stems back to about six inches in late winter or early spring, and site roots where quality, nutrient-rich soil stays moist but free-draining.

directions: This Evison introduction opens velvety plum-purple blooms with magenta shading along the midribs and paler highlights toward the crown of pale yellow stamens, gradually maturing toward a cooler bluish-purple as flowers age. It is notably free-flowering, producing blooms low on the stem as well as near the top, so the display fills in rather than concentrating at the tips. Expect repeat flowering from late spring through early fall on a vine sized for a trellis, obelisk, or large container.

common_name: Chevalier Clematis (Velvety Purple Semi-Double Compact Clematis)

planting.note: Prune lightly rather than hard in late winter to preserve some older wood, which helps this cultivar produce its characteristic semi-double and double blooms alongside single flowers.

directions: An unusual Evison introduction that can carry single, semi-double, and fully double flowers on the same plant at once, this cultivar opens velvety purple with yellow stamens and gradually lightens toward mid-blue while a red-purple midrib remains visible on each tepal. The first flush arrives in early summer, with a second wave often following in late summer into fall. Its compact, low-maintenance habit suits a small garden trellis or a large container just as well as a more traditional fence planting.
